triage.name: Hemorrhoids
triage.reason: Common anorectal complaint with bleeding and pain; diagnosis by history and exam, with important differential of rectal bleeding.

review_issues: presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Common in pregnancy and the postpartum period
More common in people with low-fiber diets and chronic constipation
Prevalence increases with age due to weakening of anal supporting tissues

risk_factors.text: Chronic constipation with straining during bowel movements

chief_complaints.text: I see bright red blood on the toilet paper after I go
There's a tender lump near my bottom
My bottom itches and feels irritated
It hurts when I sit down
Something is sticking out of my bottom after a bowel movement

hpi.onset: Gradual, often after a period of constipation or straining; external hemorrhoids can present acutely with sudden pain and a lump after thrombosis
hpi.duration: Days to weeks for acute episodes; recurrent or chronic for many patients
hpi.progression: Symptoms fluctuate with bowel habits; external hemorrhoids often improve within days, while internal hemorrhoids may progress from bleeding alone to prolapse that reduces spontaneously, then requires manual reduction, then remains prolapsed
hpi.location: Anus and lower rectum; external hemorrhoids at the anal margin, internal hemorrhoids inside the anal canal
hpi.radiation: Usually none; discomfort may be felt locally with sitting
hpi.quality: Bleeding is bright red and painless with internal hemorrhoids; external hemorrhoids cause a tender, hard lump and sharp or aching pain; itching and irritation are common
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; thrombosed external hemorrhoids can be severe (7–10/10)
hpi.timing: Bleeding typically occurs with or right after a bowel movement; pain from a thrombosed external hemorrhoid is constant and worse with sitting

associated_symptoms.text: Bright red blood on toilet paper, stool surface, or in the toilet bowl
Tender lump or swelling near the anus
Prolapse of tissue through the anus after a bowel movement

pertinent_negatives: Personal history of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease
Anemia symptoms such as fatigue or shortness of breath
Blood mixed throughout the stool rather than on the surface

positives.text: Bright red blood on toilet paper or in the toilet bowl

argues_against: Systemic symptoms such as weight loss or fever
Significant anemia from chronic blood loss

atypical.how_it_differs: Hemorrhoids are very common in the third trimester and postpartum period due to increased pelvic pressure and hormonal changes; symptoms often improve after delivery.
More likely to have internal hemorrhoids with prolapse and bleeding; must exclude colorectal cancer and other causes of rectal bleeding.
missing_classic_features: Painless bleeding as the only symptom

atypical.how_it_differs: Hemorrhoids are rare in children; rectal bleeding in a child should prompt evaluation for other causes such as anal fissure, polyp, or inflammatory bowel disease.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort when sitting; shifts position on the exam table
general.severe: Visibly uncomfortable, avoids sitting directly on the affected side, grimaces with palpation
general.critical: Not applicable; hemorrhoids are not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the perianal skin with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position, spreading the buttocks
findings.finding: One or more swollen, bluish or skin-colored nodules at the anal margin

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently palpate a perianal lump
findings.finding: Tender, firm, tense, dark bluish-purple nodule at the anal verge
Focal tenderness over an external hemorrhoid

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to strain, then inspect the anal opening
findings.finding: Reddish, mucosal-covered tissue protruding through the anus

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam with a lubricated gloved finger
findings.finding: Palpable internal hemorrhoid or enlarged anal cushions; often normal because internal hemorrhoids are soft and not always felt

findings.maneuver: Inspect the anal canal and perianal skin
findings.finding: No linear tear or ulcer at the anal verge

findings.maneuver: Palpate the perianal and ischiorectal areas
Digital rectal exam and, when indicated, anoscopy
findings.finding: No firm, irregular, or fixed mass in the anal canal or rectum
No abdominal mass, tenderness, or organomegaly
No enlarged or tender inguinal nodes

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctivae and palmar creases

labs.caveat: Usually normal; mild anemia only with chronic or heavy bleeding. Significant anemia should prompt evaluation for another source of blood loss.
Low only with chronic blood loss; supports iron deficiency from a bleeding source.
Prolonged only in patients on anticoagulants or with liver disease; helps explain bleeding severity.
Low only when an underlying hematologic or hepatic disorder is present.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected internal hemorrhoids not seen on external inspection or digital rectal exam

findings.text: Enlarged, congested anal cushions in the anal canal, typically at the left lateral, right anterior, and right posterior positions
Internal hemorrhoid that prolapses into the anoscope and reduces
No ulcerated or friable mass to suggest malignancy

imaging.preferred_when: Rectal bleeding in adults without a clear benign source, or when screening for colorectal neoplasia is due

findings.text: Normal rectal and sigmoid mucosa; hemorrhoids may be seen at the anal verge
Alternative bleeding source such as a polyp, mass, or colitis

imaging.preferred_when: Adults over 45 with rectal bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, or other alarm features; also serves as colorectal cancer screening

findings.text: Hemorrhoids at the anal canal without a proximal bleeding source
Colorectal polyp or mass found as an alternative or incidental lesion

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: Usually normal; hemorrhoids are not reliably seen
Perianal or perirectal inflammatory change if a complication such as abscess is present

initial.why: Checks for anemia from chronic or heavy rectal bleeding
Directly visualizes internal hemorrhoids and confirms the diagnosis at the bedside

supporting.why: Supports iron deficiency from chronic blood loss
supporting.only_if: anemia or heavy chronic bleeding is present

supporting.why: Assesses coagulopathy in patients on anticoagulants or with liver disease
supporting.only_if: bleeding is unusually heavy or the patient is anticoagulated

supporting.why: Excludes colorectal cancer and other proximal bleeding sources
supporting.only_if: age over 45, iron deficiency anemia, alarm features, or bleeding not explained by hemorrhoids

supporting.why: Evaluates the distal colon when colonoscopy is not available or not indicated
supporting.only_if: rectal bleeding without a clear benign source

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for uncomplicated hemorrhoids; reserved for suspected abscess or other complication
Not helpful unless an inflammatory or infectious process is suspected
Not part of hemorrhoid workup unless pregnancy affects management decisions

decision_points: Confirm the bleeding source with anoscopy or endoscopy before attributing rectal bleeding to hemorrhoids in adults over 45 or with alarm features
Check hemoglobin in anyone with heavy or chronic bleeding
Consider colonoscopy for rectal bleeding when colorectal cancer screening is due or alarm symptoms are present

differential.name: Colorectal cancer
differential.why_considered: Rectal bleeding is the most common presenting symptom, and hemorrhoids are a frequent incidental finding that can distract from a proximal malignancy.
differential.trigger: Rectal bleeding in an adult over 45, or any patient with iron deficiency anemia, weight loss, or a change in stool caliber

history: Age over 45 or due for colorectal cancer screening
Unintentional weight loss
Change in stool caliber or frequency
Family history of colorectal cancer
Bleeding mixed with stool rather than only on the surface
exam: Firm, irregular, or fixed mass on digital rectal exam
Pallor or signs of chronic illness
labs: Iron deficiency anemia with low ferritin
Occult blood positive on stool testing
imaging: Colonoscopy showing a mass, polyp, or stricture

differential.name: Anal fissure
differential.why_considered: Causes bright red rectal bleeding and severe anal pain, especially with bowel movements, and often coexists with constipation.

history: Sharp, tearing pain during and after bowel movements lasting minutes to hours
History of hard stools or constipation
Pain out of proportion to the amount of bleeding
exam: Linear tear or ulcer in the anal canal, typically at the posterior midline
Severe tenderness that limits digital rectal exam
Sentinel skin tag or hypertrophied anal papilla
imaging: Anoscopy may be deferred due to pain; diagnosis is usually clinical

differential.name: Perianal abscess
differential.why_considered: Presents with a painful perianal lump and swelling that can be mistaken for a thrombosed external hemorrhoid.
differential.trigger: Fever, severe constant pain, and a fluctuant, warm, indurated perianal mass

history: Constant, throbbing pain unrelated to bowel movements
Fever and chills
History of Crohn disease or diabetes
exam: No bluish-purple thrombosed nodule at the anal verge
imaging: CT or endoanal ultrasound showing a fluid collection if the diagnosis is unclear

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
differential.why_considered: Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis can cause rectal bleeding, tenesmus, and perianal symptoms, and hemorrhoids may be a secondary finding.

history: Chronic diarrhea, urgency, and tenesmus
Weight loss and fatigue
Extraintestinal symptoms such as joint pain or rash
exam: Perianal skin tags, fistulas, or fissures
imaging: Colonoscopy with continuous mucosal inflammation, ulceration, or skip lesions

differential.name: Rectal prolapse
differential.why_considered: Tissue protruding from the anus after a bowel movement can be mistaken for a prolapsed internal hemorrhoid.

history: Full-thickness protrusion that may require manual reduction
Fecal incontinence or mucus discharge
More common in older women with pelvic floor weakness
exam: Concentric folds of rectal mucosa visible on straining
Prolapse that may be reducible or incarcerated
imaging: Defecography or dynamic MRI if the diagnosis is uncertain

differential.name: Anal cancer
differential.why_considered: Can present with rectal bleeding, anal pain, and a mass that may be attributed to hemorrhoids.
differential.trigger: Firm, irregular anal mass, persistent bleeding, or risk factors such as HPV infection or immunosuppression

history: Persistent anal pain or bleeding not responding to hemorrhoid treatment
History of HPV, HIV, or immunosuppression
Sensation of a mass
exam: Firm, irregular, or ulcerated mass in the anal canal

severity.mild: Grade I internal hemorrhoids with bleeding only, or small external hemorrhoids with mild itching and discomfort; symptoms controlled with conservative measures
severity.moderate: Grade II–III internal hemorrhoids with prolapse that reduces spontaneously or requires manual reduction, or thrombosed external hemorrhoids with significant pain; may require office procedures
severity.severe: Grade IV internal hemorrhoids that are irreducible or chronically prolapsed, or recurrent thrombosed external hemorrhoids; may require surgical hemorrhoidectomy
severity.critical: Not applicable; hemorrhoids are not a life-threatening condition, though severe bleeding can rarely cause significant anemia

red_flags.finding: Rectal bleeding in an adult over 45 or with iron deficiency anemia
red_flags.meaning: Must exclude colorectal cancer; do not attribute bleeding to hemorrhoids without evaluation

red_flags.finding: Weight loss, change in stool caliber, or systemic symptoms
red_flags.meaning: Suggests malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease

red_flags.finding: Fever, severe constant pain, and a fluctuant perianal mass
Irreducible prolapsed hemorrhoid with severe pain and swelling
red_flags.meaning: Strangulated or thrombosed hemorrhoid; urgent surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: Significant anemia or hemodynamic instability from rectal bleeding
red_flags.meaning: Severe blood loss; evaluate for another source and resuscitate

complications.name: Thrombosis of external hemorrhoid
clues: Tender, firm, bluish-purple nodule at the anal verge

complications.name: Chronic blood loss with iron deficiency anemia

special_populations.differences: Very common in the third trimester and postpartum period due to increased pelvic pressure and hormonal changes; symptoms often improve after delivery. Treatment is conservative, with stool softeners and sitz baths; surgery is avoided unless necessary.

More likely to have internal hemorrhoids with prolapse and bleeding; must exclude colorectal cancer and other causes of rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy is recommended for rectal bleeding in adults over 45.
Hemorrhoids are rare in children; rectal bleeding should prompt evaluation for anal fissure, polyp, or inflammatory bowel disease rather than assuming hemorrhoids.
Higher risk of perianal infections and abscesses; a low threshold for imaging and surgical consultation is warranted.

key_questions.question: What does the bleeding look like — is it bright red on the toilet paper or dripping into the bowl, or is it mixed in with the stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Bright red blood on the surface of the stool, on toilet paper, or dripping into the bowl after a bowel movement; blood mixed throughout the stool suggests a more proximal source

key_questions.question: Is the bleeding painful or painless?
key_questions.looking_for: Painless bleeding with internal hemorrhoids; severe sharp pain with a bowel movement suggests an anal fissure

key_questions.question: Is there a lump or tissue coming out of your bottom, and does it go back in on its own?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolapse that reduces spontaneously, requires manual reduction, or stays out — this grades internal hemorrhoids and guides treatment

key_questions.question: How long has this been going on, and is it getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Days to weeks for acute episodes; progressive prolapse over months suggests advancing internal hemorrhoids

key_questions.question: What makes it worse — straining, sitting on the toilet, long periods of sitting?
key_questions.looking_for: Straining with bowel movements, prolonged toilet sitting, and heavy lifting increase pressure on the anal cushions

key_questions.question: How often do you have a bowel movement, and what is the stool like — hard, soft, or loose?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic constipation with hard stools and straining, or chronic diarrhea; both are strong risk factors

key_questions.question: How much fiber and fluid do you get in a typical day?
key_questions.looking_for: Low-fiber diet and inadequate fluid intake, which are modifiable contributors

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any itching, irritation, mucus discharge, or soiling around the anus?
key_questions.looking_for: Anal itching, irritation, mucus discharge, or soiling from prolapsed internal hemorrhoids

key_questions.question: Have you had any weight loss, change in stool caliber, dark or tarry stools, or abdominal pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Alarm features that suggest colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease rather than hemorrhoids

key_questions.question: Is there any personal or family history of colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, or colon polyps?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk factors that lower the threshold for colonoscopy and make attributing bleeding to hemorrhoids unsafe

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have anemia, or do you feel fatigued or short of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss

key_questions.question: Are you pregnant, or have you recently given birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy and the postpartum period are common times for hemorrhoids to appear or worsen

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including any blood thinners or opioids?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticoagulants that worsen bleeding; opioids and other constipating drugs that promote straining

key_questions.question: Have you tried any home treatments, and did they help?
key_questions.looking_for: Response to fiber, stool softeners, sitz baths, and topical creams; persistent symptoms after a week of treatment warrant evaluation

reasoning_points: Bright red blood on the toilet paper, stool surface, or in the toilet bowl after a bowel movement
Painless bleeding with internal hemorrhoids; a tender, hard lump with sharp pain suggests a thrombosed external hemorrhoid
Tissue protruding from the anus after a bowel movement, which may reduce spontaneously or require manual reduction
Anal itching, irritation, or mucus discharge
Risk factors such as chronic constipation, straining, low-fiber diet, prolonged toilet sitting, pregnancy, or heavy lifting
Perianal inspection showing swollen nodules at the anal margin, or anoscopy showing enlarged anal cushions
No alarm features such as weight loss, change in stool caliber, dark stools, or systemic symptoms
No firm, irregular, or fixed mass on digital rectal exam or anoscopy
Colorectal cancer excluded in adults over 45 or with iron deficiency anemia before attributing bleeding to hemorrhoids

easy: Classic painless bright red bleeding on toilet paper after a bowel movement
Visible external hemorrhoid or palpable internal hemorrhoid on exam
No alarm features and normal hemoglobin
medium: Prolapsed internal hemorrhoid that requires manual reduction
Thrombosed external hemorrhoid with a tender bluish-purple nodule and severe pain
Coexisting anal fissure causing sharp pain with bowel movements
hard: Older adult with rectal bleeding and iron deficiency anemia where colorectal cancer must be excluded
Patient on anticoagulation with heavy bleeding and a normal exam
Pregnant patient in the third trimester with prolapse and discomfort
Rectal prolapse or anal cancer mimicking a prolapsed hemorrhoid
Immunocompromised patient with perianal pain and a possible abscess
